div.p: Noninvasive genetic sampling is an essential tool for studying elusive and endangered species. However, the DNA from noninvasive genetic sampling tends to be low in quantity and quality, which leads to poor DNA amplification. Using fecal pellets of pygmy rabbits (Brachylagus idahoensis) collected in February, March, and November 2011, we tested a possible solution of increasing the amount of sample by combining multiple pellet groups during DNA extraction. One potential drawback of this approach is accidental mixing of samples from multiple species. This study evaluates the mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) species identification success rate for pygmy rabbit (PY) fecal DNA when mixed with eastern cottontail (Sylvilagus floridanus; EC) fecal pellet DNA at lower frequencies (1PY:3EC and 2PY:6EC) and eastern cottontail or mountain cottontail (S. nuttalli) pellet samples at an equal frequency (4:4). We found that successful detection of pygmy rabbit DNA using a species-specific mtDNA polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test varies from 0% to 95% depending on the competing species and PCR protocol. From these results, we conclude that if samples are unintentionally mixed, the species with a greater number of pellets within the sample will be more likely to be detected. Also, if pellet piles are intentionally mixed to reduce sampling cost, the protocol should be optimized to maximize DNA amplification for the focal species; however, there will be reduced detection rates depending on the quality and quantity of the focal species DNA within the sample.

Noninvasive genetic sampling is an important tool for studying and monitoring wildlife populations and is particularly useful for elusive and endangered species that are difficult to capture (Taberlet et al. 1999, Waits andPaetkau 2005). Obtaining DNA from hair, feces, and other sources allows minimal disruption of the focal species, and is cost-efficient compared with more invasive methods (Goossens et al. 1998, Taberlet et al. 1999, Sloane et al. 2000, Beja-Pereira et al. 2009). Noninvasive genetic sampling enables researchers to determine species identification, individual identification, species distribution, species abundance, and important population genetic parameters (Waits andPaetkau 2005, Beja-Pereira et al. 2009). Despite the advantages of noninvasive genetic sampling, noninvasive DNA sources tend to have low-quantity and low-quality DNA, which often leads to low DNA-amplification success rates and high microsatellite-genotyping error rates (Tab-erlet et al. 1999, Parsons 2001, Alpers et al. 2003, Waits and Paetkau 2005). Two solutions to this problem include collecting fresh samples and increasing the amount of the sample by combining multiple hairs or multiple fecal pellets (Foran et al. 1997, Goossens et al. 1998, Woods et al. 1999, Flagstad et al. 2004, Adams et al. 2011). Using multiple hairs or fecal pellets per sample may improve the quantity and quality of extracted DNA, but this could lead to mixing of samples between multiple species or multiple individuals (Woods et al. 1999, Roon et al. 2005).

Researchers have evaluated the impact of mixing samples from multiple individuals when conducting microsatellite analysis and individual identification (Alpers et al. 2003, Roon et al. 2005). Both studies found that this type of error is likely to be detected because multiple alleles (!3) will be observed at a single locus. A few studies have reported detecting multiple species in hair collected noninvasively (Woods et al. 1999, Mowat andStrobeck 2000), and one study has empirically evaluated the impact of mixing hair samples from 2 species on the ability to detect the DNA of Delmarva fox squirrels (Sciurus niger cinereus; Moncrief et al. 2008).

Recently, Adams et al. (2011) developed a mitochondrial DNA species identification test to differentiate the pygmy rabbit (Brachylagus idahoensis) from other sympatric rabbit species. The size and morphology of pygmy rabbit fecal pellets change throughout the year, and they can be difficult to distinguish from other lagomorph species, particularly the eastern (Sylvilagus floridanus) and mountain (S. nuttallii) cottontails (Larrucea andBrussard 2008, Adams et al. 2011).

However, DNA extraction of multiple fecal pellets (>3) is necessary to have enough DNA to achieve high species-ID success rates (Adams et al. 2011). Managers have considered cutting costs of noninvasive genetic sampling surveys for pygmy rabbits by pooling samples from multiple pellet piles, thereby reducing the number of samples that need to be analyzed from each sampling location. However, collecting from multiple pellet piles increases the chance to misidentify the pellets and mix multiple lagomorph species into one sample. Thus, it is important to evaluate the impact of mixing pellets from different species on species identification rates. This study evaluates the ability of a species-specific polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test to detect pygmy rabbit DNA when pygmy rabbit (PY) fecal pellets are mixed with fecal pellets of eastern (EC) and mountain cottontail (MC) rabbits. Our first objective was to evaluate the ability of an established PCR protocol (Adams et al. 2011) to detect pygmy rabbit DNA when pygmy rabbit pellets are at a lower frequency (1PY:3EC and 2PY:6EC) and equal frequency (4PY:4EC) compared with eastern cottontail pellets. Our second objective was to evaluate whether PY detection success rates can be increased using alternative PCR protocols and whether the identity of the species (ET or MC) influences success rates when pellet numbers are held equal (4:4).

div.head: Fecal Pellet Sampling
div.p: The pygmy rabbit, eastern cottontail rabbit, and mountain cottontail rabbit used in this study were held in a captive facility at Washington State University in Pullman, WA, USA. All animal care protocols were approved under Washington State University Animal Care and Use Protocol no. 3994. We collected pellets from trays under the cages and placed them outside for 48 hr to simulate the DNA degradation that occurs under field conditions. After 48 hr, we collected pellets in coin envelopes and placed them in Ziploc bags containing silica desiccant to preserve the DNA until extraction.

There were 5 collection periods, and for each collection period the high and low temperatures and the amount of precipitation was recorded from the Pullman/Moscow Regional Airport using data from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration website (http://www.noaa. gov/wx.html). Collection periods 1 and 2 were done in February 2011 with average high and low temperatures of 38C and À138C with light snowfall (<13 mm). Collection period 3 was in March 2011 with average high and low temperatures of 138C and 08C with light rainfall (approx. 4 mm). Collection periods 4 and 5 were done in November 2011 with average high and low temperatures of 88C and À68C and light rainfall (approx. 4 mm).

div.head: Laboratory Protocols
div.p: For objective 1, we used pellets collected from periods 1-3 in 2 different 1:3 ratios (1PY:3EC, 2PY:6EC) and a 1:1 ratio (4PY:4EC) for DNA extraction. Twenty samples of the appropriate ratio were constructed for each test and extracted using the QIAamp DNA Stool Mini Kit (Qiagen, Inc.) according to the manufacturer's protocol with one exception. For the 2PY:6EC and 4PY:4EC pellet ratios, we used 2,400 ml of ASL lysis buffer (QIAamp Kit) to insure that all pellets were saturated with buffer. We conducted DNA extractions in a laboratory dedicated to low-quantity DNA sources and included negative controls to test for contamination. The PCR profile used for all ratios in objective 1 (1PY:3EC, 2PY:6EC, 4PY:4EC) amplifies a portion of the mitochondrial DNA cytochrome b (CytB) gene as described in Adams et al. (2011). This PCR multiplex was designed to distinguish all rabbit species in the pygmy rabbit range and included 1 ml of fecal DNA extract, 1.2 mM of RabCytb universal F primer, 0.04 mM PY reverse primer, 0.2 mM EC reverse primer, 0.6 mM of the MC R primer, 0.25 mM of the black-tailed jackrabbit (Lepus californicus) R primer and 0.2 mM of the white-tailed jackrabbit (L. townsendii) reverse primer. Although jackrabbit samples were not a part of this study, they were left in the multiplex because it was originally designed to discriminate all sympatric rabbit species and all primers will be used when this test is implemented in the field. We separated PCR products (1 ml) on a 3130xl Applied Biosystems Genetic Analyzer and used GeneMapper 3.7 software (Applied Biosystems, Inc., Foster City, CA) for fragment analysis. A band observed in the 294-basepair size range above 75 fluorescent units was considered a success for PY amplification. A band in the 177-basepair size range above 75 fluorescent units was considered a success for EC amplification.

For objective 2, we used pellets collected from periods 3 to 5 to create 20 samples using a 1:1 ratio (4PY:4EC and 4PY:4MC) for DNA extraction. The same DNA extraction protocol was used as previously described in objective 1. We tested 2 alternative PCR protocols that included 1 ml of fecal DNA extract and the same conditions described in Adams et al. (2011) with changes in the amount of the speciesspecific mitochondrial DNA cytochrome b primers that favored amplification of pygmy rabbit DNA compared with the protocol used for objective 1. In the equal-primerconcentration PCR protocol (hereafter known as the Even PCR protocol), we changed all species-specific primers to equal concentrations (0.2 mM). In the pygmy-rabbit-specific PCR protocol, hereby known as PY-Specific PCR, the MCand EC-specific primers were lowered to 0.05 mM, and the PY-specific and jackrabbit-specific primers remained at 0.2 mM. We analyzed and interpreted PCR products as described for objective 1. For the fragment analysis of MC, a band in the 172-basepair size range above 75 fluorescent units was considered a successful amplification. The fragment size and fluorescent units for PY and EC were the same as in objective 1.

div.head: Statistical Analyses
div.p: We used the Fisher's Exact statistical test (R version 2.15.1; R Core Team 2012) to test whether there was significant improvement in PY DNA detection in the 2 altered protocols compared with the established PCR protocol and to compare the detection rates of PY DNA with other lagomorph species.

div.head: RESULTS
div.p: For objective 1, we detected PY DNA in 2 samples (10%) for the 1PY:3EC ratio and 0 samples for the 2PY:6EC ratio (Table 1). For the 4PY:4EC ratio, we detected PY DNA in 4 samples (20%; Table 1), which was not significantly higher than the 1:3 ratio (P ¼ 0.661) or the 2:6 ratio (P ¼ 0.106). For the 1PY:3EC ratio, we detected EC DNA in 17 samples (85%), and EC DNA detection rates were 100% for the 2PY:6EC and 4PY:4EC ratios. In all comparisons, EC DNA was more likely to amplify than PY DNA (P < 0.05). The average fluorescent units for PY ranged from 222 to 391; whereas, the EC average fluorescent units ranged from 1,877 to 6,414 (Table 1).

For the Even PCR protocol, we detected PY DNA for 16 samples (80%) for both the 4PY:4EC ratio and the 4PY:4MC ratio (Table 2). We detected MC DNA in 15 samples (75%) and EC DNA in 100% of samples (Table 2). This altered PCR protocol was significantly more likely to detect pygmy rabbit DNA than the original protocol used for objective 1 (P < 0.001). There was not a significant difference in our ability to detect PY versus EC (P ¼ 0.106) or PY versus MC (P ¼ 1.0) using this PCR profile with even concentrations of species-specific primers. For the PY-Specific PCR protocol, we detected PY DNA in 17 samples (85%) for the 4PY:4EC ratio and 19 samples (95%) for the 4PY:4MC ratio (Table 2). This was a significant improvement in pygmy rabbit identification success rates when comparing the 4PY:4EC original PCR protocol to the 4PY:4EC PY-Specific PCR protocol (P < 0.001). However, there was not a significant improvement when comparing the Even PCR protocol for either 4PY:4MC (P ¼ 0.342) or 4PY:4EC (P ¼ 1.0). We detected MC DNA in 16 samples (80%) and EC DNA in all 20 samples (100%) under the PY-Specific PCR protocol (Table 2). Although we significantly decreased the primer concentrations for EC and MC compared with PY, we did not detect a decline in success rates for amplifying EC (P ¼ 1.0) or MC (P ¼ 1.0) DNA compared with the Even PCR protocol. There was not a significant difference in our ability to detect PY versus EC (P ¼ 0.231) and PY versus MC (P ¼ 0.342) using the PY-Specific PCR profile.

The intensity of PCR amplification for PY was highest for the PY-Specific PCR protocol based on fluorescent unit averages, while the greatest fluorescent intensities for EC and MC were observed under the Even PCR protocol (Tables 1 and2). Across all PCR profiles, EC DNA amplified at a higher intensity than PY DNA, while PY DNA amplified at a higher intensity than MC DNA for both the Even PCR and PY-Specific PCR profiles (Tables 1 and2).

div.head: DISCUSSION
div.p: We found that successful amplification of target species from mixed-species samples of fecal pellets varies considerably (0-95%) depending on the PCR protocol, number of pellets, and relative ratio of target to nontarget species pellets. By increasing the number of pellets/species and adjusting the PCR protocol to preferentially amplify the focal species, we were able to increase the detection rate to >85% in mixedspecies pellet groups when pellets from both species were at Table 1. div.head: Ratio
div.p: even concentrations. We were unable to find any other studies that compared species ID success rates for mixed fecal samples but one study demonstrated that a single hair sample from a target species could be consistently detected when mixed with 19 hairs of a nontarget species (Moncrief et al. 2008).

There are several variables that may explain why we did not obtain 100% pygmy rabbit detection from mixed-species groups of fecal pellets including DNA degradation due to weather conditions, differences in PCR product length and the efficiency and/or strength of primer binding, and differences in the number of pellets per species. During the 48 hr that the pellets were in the field, DNA was degrading as they were exposed to rain and snow, and multiple studies have shown that DNA degrades rapidly after deposition (Kovach et al. 2003, Piggott 2004, Murphy et al. 2007, Santini et al. 2007, Panasci et al. 2011), and increased moisture decreases PCR success rates for fecal DNA (Lucchini et al. 2002, Murphy et al. 2007, Santini et al. 2007).

To minimize the effects of DNA degradation and increase fecal DNA success rates, researchers have suggested that PCR amplicons should be <200 basepairs (Taberlet et al. 1999, Beja-Pereira et al. 2009). Both species-specific PCR products for eastern and mountain cottontail were <200 basepairs but the pygmy rabbit-specific reverse primer produces a fragment that is 294 basepairs long, which may explain the lower success rates for this species. To improve the probability of pygmy rabbit DNA amplification, one possibility would be redesigning this primer set to amplify a shorter fragment. However, efforts to do this have been unsuccessful because of a lack of species-specific priming sites for this species in this region of CytB. The number of pellets in the extraction and the relative ratio of each species are also important variables in mixed-species experiments. We found very low success rates when using only 1-2 pellets/species and when pygmy rabbit pellets were outnumbered 1:3 by nontarget species pellets. These results are consistent with the findings of Adams et al. (2011), who indicated that !4 fecal pellets were required for high success rates for pygmy rabbit species ID.

The results highlight the risks of failing to detect pygmy rabbits (or any target species of interest) when mixing pellet groups that include multiple species. We suggest increasing the number of pellets extracted per sample when purposefully combining samples from different pellet groups to decrease the cost of analyses or when there is a high probability that multiple species may be represented in a single sample collected in the field. The challenges of detecting the target species in a mixed-species group are also likely to be greater under field conditions where the age of samples and the relative ratios of target to nontarget species are unknown. If pooling samples from different pellet groups is desirable or if pellets are intermixed in a way that is not possible to distinguish different pellet groups, we recommend using a minimum of 8 pellets/extraction and using the PY-Specific PCR protocol to increase the probability of successful detection of pygmy rabbits.

div.head: MANAGEMENT IMPLICATIONS
div.p: Our results suggests that managers may use the technique of pooling pellets from multiple pellet piles (4 pellets/pile) in order to determine the presence of lagomorph species. Mangers should realize that this method would not provide 100% successful species detection, but if the goal is to sample large areas for lagomorph presence this pooling technique may be beneficial by lowering the sample analysis expenses.
